t649cc9b20: Under the LGPD (Brazil’s General Data Protection Law), art. 46 requires security measures that protect personal data from unauthorized access and from alteration, loss or destruction. Art. 37 requires controllers and processors to keep records of their processing operations, and the accountability principle, set out in art. 6, item X, requires showing that the measures adopted are effective. A verifiable trail is a concrete way to make that showing.

t8ae34899c: Almost every system keeps some kind of log. The question an experienced auditor asks is a different one: “How do I know nobody tampered with these records?” A hash-chained audit trail exists to answer that question with a verification, not a request for trust.
t96a3ffdd1: Someone deletes the latest records: the system separately stores which record was written last and its fingerprint. If the end of the chain doesn’t match that reference, the verification warns that the most recent records were deleted.

ta0120467e: On the dashboard, you can filter by event, user and period and export the result as CSV. The export includes each record’s fingerprint and that of the previous one, and timestamps are in UTC to avoid time zone confusion. It is also protected against formulas: if a value starts with characters such as “=”, “+”, “-” or “@” — for example, a malicious username typed into a login attempt — the file stores it as text, and the spreadsheet won’t run it as a formula.
tab34a99ce: The verification walks the chain from the first record to the last and, if it finds a problem, reports the first affected record and the reason. The verification itself is also logged in the trail, with its date and result.

tccd0f8fb6: Where this meets ISO/IEC 27001 and the LGPD
tcdebde9f0: Each record in the trail stores who did it, what, on which object, when, from which IP address and browser, plus the event details. From that content, the system calculates a SHA-256 hash: a 64-character fingerprint that changes completely if any detail changes.
td71f65219: During the audit, the auditor asks how anyone can know the permissions history hasn’t been edited. The administrator opens the audit screen and clicks “Verify integrity now.” The result appears with the date, time and number of records checked. Next, they filter the audited period, export the CSV and hand over the file. Both the verification and the export are logged in the trail itself.
tea50f473c: ISO/IEC 27001:2022 includes, in Annex A, control 8.15 on logging: logs recording activities, exceptions, faults and other relevant events must be produced, stored, protected and analyzed. Hash chaining directly addresses the “protected” part, with a verification you can demonstrate to the auditor.
tf2f4ecd8f: In most systems, the log is just a table in the database. Anyone with database access can edit a row, change a date or delete an entire event — and nothing shows that it happened. Backups help, but rarely does anyone compare the current log with an old copy.

tfc2de9c69: In the current version, the trail automatically logs logins, logouts and failed attempts, user creation and deletion, role changes, plugin activation and deactivation, license events, modules turned on and off, as well as the trail’s own verifications and exports.
